```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(reiod)
```

**Start here.** Every other article assumes your impact values are the right
type, the right unit and the right precision. They very often are not, and
when they are not the metrics do not complain — they return a confidently
wrong number.

That is the whole reason this page comes before the ones on computing
anything. A unit error does not look like an error. It looks like a result.

## The one check that is automatic, and the many that are not

**Only one test runs on the default path.** The metric functions refuse an
integer impact vector, because `is.numeric(1L)` is `TRUE` and nothing else
would catch it:

```{r, error = TRUE}
grp <- eiod_age_sex_group(eiod_demo$age, eiod_demo$sex)
eiod_absolute_threshold(as.integer(eiod_demo$land_arable_m2yr), grp,
                        "landarable")
```

Everything else — sign, zeros, unit magnitude, retained significant digits,
cut-off proximity — happens **only if you ask**. The checks report rather than
stop, so one pass finds every problem instead of making you fix them one at a
time.

## The one call that runs them all

`eiod_check_data()` runs six component checks over a whole data frame:

```{r}
report <- eiod_check_data(
  eiod_demo,
  impacts = c(biodiv = "biodiv_pdf", ghg = "ghg_kgco2e"),
  age = "age", sex = "sex", gdqs = "gdqs"
)
summary(report)
```

The `impacts` argument is the same named-vector idea used everywhere in
`reiod`: the **name** is the indicator key, the **value** is your column. You
can check any subset.

Print the report rather than summarising it to see each finding in full:

```{r}
report
```

## The two checks worth understanding

### Unit magnitude

This is the one that would have caught every real-world mistake we have seen.
It compares your median against the published global reference and, when the
ratio lands near a known conversion factor, names the conversion:

```{r}
eiod_check_magnitude(eiod_demo$ghg_kgco2e * 1000, "ghg", grp,
                     name = "ghg_in_grams")
```

A factor of 1000 is the common one — grams where kilograms are expected, or
the reverse. Note that eutrophication is the indicator where this is easiest
to get wrong, and the one place `reiod` expects **grams**; see
`vignette("eutrophication")`.

### Precision

R's `numeric` is a double, so a biodiversity value of `3.6896e-13` is
comfortably representable and `<` comparison against a cut-off is exact. **The
small exponent is not the problem.**

The risk is ingestion fidelity — what happened to the number before it reached
R. Excel re-saving displayed digits. A CSV export written at six significant
digits. Stata `float` storage. A database `REAL` column. The check measures how
many significant digits a column has actually retained, and counts how many
observations sit close enough to their own cut-off that the lost digits could
flip the classification:

```{r}
eiod_check_precision(eiod_demo$water_litres, grp, "water",
                     name = "water_litres")
```

The companion Stata implementation measured this on 200,000 simulated
respondent-days. Single-precision storage changed **0 of 200,000** absolute
classifications and **1 of 200,000** relative bands — while **integer** storage
of greenhouse gas emissions biased the mean down by **13%**. The intuition that
the tiny exponent is the danger turns out to be the wrong worry. Truncation is
the real one.

`vignette("precision")` works through how to decide whether lost digits matter
for *your* data. Run it before you generate any indicator.

## The recommended pre-flight block

```r
library(reiod)

# 1. state which column holds which indicator, once
my_map <- c(ghg = "ghg_kgco2e", biodiv = "biodiv_pdf")

# 2. the demographic group
grp <- eiod_age_sex_group(mydata$age, mydata$sex)

# 3. the full suite: type, sign, zeros, unit magnitude, precision
summary(eiod_check_data(mydata, impacts = my_map,
                        age = "age", sex = "sex", gdqs = "gdqs"))

# 4. precision per indicator, against the cut-off that will actually be used
for (ind in names(my_map)) {
  print(eiod_check_precision(mydata[[my_map[[ind]]]], grp, ind, name = my_map[[ind]]))
}

# 5. only now generate the indicators
```

## What the checks cannot do

**Incomplete EIOF coverage.** Not every food has an impact factor. A food
without one contributes nothing to the day total, so the total is understated —
and `reiod` cannot detect it, because it receives one number per
respondent-day and the aggregation has already discarded the evidence.

Count the share of consumed weight carrying an impact factor when you
aggregate, and report it alongside any prevalence. The one detectable case —
every food uncosted, summing to `0` rather than `NA` — is caught by the zero
check. `vignette("troubleshooting")` has the full discussion.
